questions.q: Why does cause-based alerting (e.g. 'CPU above 80%') tend to generate more alert fatigue than symptom-based alerting?
options: Because CPU metrics are harder to collect than latency metrics
Because the underlying cause can fluctuate without actually affecting users, so it fires even when nothing customer-facing is broken
Because cause-based alerts always have the wrong severity
Because symptom-based alerts cannot be automated
questions.explain: High CPU isn't inherently a problem — it only matters if it's actually degrading something users experience. Cause-based alerts fire on fluctuations that don't always translate into real impact, generating noise.

questions.q: What is the practical test for whether an alert should page a human at all?
options: Whether it is technically possible to measure the underlying metric
Whether, if woken up for it, there is something specific the person can and should do immediately
Whether the alert has fired at least three times before
Whether a dashboard already shows the same data
questions.explain: An alert should only page someone if it's actionable — if there's nothing to do right now, it belongs on a dashboard or in a digest, not as a page.

questions.q: What problem does alert grouping/deduplication solve?
options: It reduces the total number of metrics a system collects
It prevents one root cause from appearing as many separate unrelated alerts, which otherwise costs time just figuring out they're the same incident
It automatically assigns an incident commander
It eliminates the need for severity levels
questions.explain: Without grouping, one underlying cause that affects twelve services can trigger twelve separate pages, forcing the responder to waste time realizing they're all the same incident.

questions.q: How does an SLO burn-rate alert differ from a raw threshold alert like 'error rate > 1%'?
options: It ignores errors entirely and only tracks latency
It only fires when the error rate is high enough, for long enough, to meaningfully threaten the SLO's error budget — filtering out brief blips that recover on their own
It requires no configuration and works identically to a raw threshold
It can only be used for SEV1 incidents
questions.explain: A burn-rate alert ties alerting to how fast the error budget is being consumed relative to the SLO, which naturally filters out short-lived blips while still catching sustained real problems.

questions.q: Why is alert fatigue described as 'a design problem, not a personal failing'?
options: Because on-call engineers are never responsible for responding to alerts
Because the root cause is how alerts were defined (what they alert on, whether they're actionable, whether they're grouped) rather than an individual's attentiveness
Because alert fatigue cannot actually be measured
Because only automated systems can experience alert fatigue
questions.explain: Fatigue results from poorly designed alerting — cause-based triggers, non-actionable pages, lack of grouping — not from an individual engineer failing to pay attention. Fixing the design fixes the fatigue.
